BLOCKER: Acceptance criterion "delete/replica/backup reconciliation job" is unmet: only a library `objreconcile.Scan` exists — no job entrypoint, scheduler, CLI, or call site anywhere in the diff, so drift is never actually detected/reported in production.

The signed-URL tenant boundary is spoofable: `objpolicy.WithTenant` is exported and applied via plain context value, so any downstream handler/middleware can overwrite the "authenticated" tenant after `HTTPMiddleware` and Mint will honor it; the ADR claim "never a caller argument" is not enforced by the type system.

Signed-URL minting allows mutating methods (`PUT`, `DELETE`) with up to 15-minute TTL; a leaked/pasted URL is a scoped write/delete primitive with no per-tenant rate limit or revocation path — fail-closed posture is inconsistent with the rest of the design.
MAJOR: `objreconcile.MaxObjects` does not actually prevent OOM: `store.List` already materializes the full listing into a slice before the bound check, so the stated "fail closed rather than OOM on bucket-scale listings" guarantee is false; pagination/streaming is required.

No shared provider conformance suite: S3 has an ad-hoc integration test and local has ad-hoc unit tests, but there is no parameterized conformance harness run per provider, so lifecycle semantics can silently diverge between adapters (reuse + criterion coverage gap).
`HTTPMiddleware` has zero wiring into the actual API server and no end-to-end test proving Mint is only reachable behind auth; the privilege boundary exists only in unit tests with a stub resolver.

`LocalStore.lockFor` map grows unbounded per key and is never evicted: long-lived processes with many distinct keys leak memory and mutexes; also only protects within a single process (multi-writer/TOCTOU across processes is unaddressed and undocumented).

S3 `Immutable` without retention relies on a startup-time versioning probe that can go stale (bucket config changed later) and silently weakens the immutability guarantee; revalidation or a documented operational control is needed.
MINOR: `S3Store.Capabilities` acquires `lockMu` twice separately, yielding a non-atomic snapshot of `objectLock`/`versioned`; use one critical section.
`ObjectLifecycle` does not lazily re-probe lock config the way `ApplyLifecycle` does, so a valid bucket reports `ErrUnsupported` until process restart — inconsistent capability discovery.
`probeLock` logs a failure line on every `ApplyLifecycle` retry against a lock-less bucket (unbounded log growth under a retry loop).
`objreconcile.Scan` returns a partially-filled `Report` alongside an error on transient `Head` failure; callers that ignore the error get an incomplete report presented as authoritative.

Drift report has no run identity (timestamp, duration, store provider, manifest source), which hurts observability/correlation while preserving determinism; emit run metadata outside the deterministic arrays.
`objpolicy.Stats()` keys include raw tenant IDs; exporting these as metric labels leaks tenant identity and risks unbounded label cardinality in the metrics backend.

`S3Store.stat`/`Delete` now translate `NoSuchKey` to `os.ErrNotExist`, a behavior change for existing callers of `Get`/`Head`/`Delete` that is not covered by adapter-level tests or noted outside the ADR.

Retention-at-Put is rejected on `Retention < time.Minute` with `ErrInvalidPolicy` while `objpolicy` TTL bounds are separate constants; consider one shared policy-bounds module to avoid future divergence.
NIT: `errLocalLifecycle` declared as `var x error = &...` instead of a typed value or `errors.New`-style sentinel; the intermediate interface type adds no value.
`objreconcile.notFound` is a one-line wrapper around `errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist)`; fine today but worth consolidating with the datastore error vocabulary once S3/local mappings firm up.
`deny()` overflow bucket `_overflow|reason` still keys on tenant-less reason but silently drops tenant attribution; document that overflow counts are global.
`TestScanAbortsOnTransientHeadError` builds an unused `st` fixture and discards it with `_ = st`; delete the dead setup.
SUMMARY: Solid foundations: capability-gated lifecycle interface, fail-closed local adapter, central minting with TTL bounds, sha256-based read-only reconciliation, and full Go compliance with L1 — no language-rule violations.

Top risks against acceptance: the reconciliation "job" does not exist (only a library function), the signed-URL tenant context is spoofable via an exported setter, and mutating signed URLs are permitted — these must be closed before the item can ship.
Secondary: no shared per-provider conformance harness, the MaxObjects bound does not bound memory, and the middleware is unwired, leaving the security boundary unproven end-to-end.
